samples.summary: `READ_GATED_METHODS` downgrades `AttachDocument` to a read check, so a share-link `viewer` can write arbitrary content by carrying a change pack in the attach itself
samples.evidence:
Before this change `checkAttribute` computed `needWrite = attr.verb === 'rw' || REVISION_READ_METHODS.has(method)`, so an `AttachDocument` (which Yorkie always sends with verb `rw`) required `link.role === 'editor'`. The new expression at yorkie-auth.controller.ts:332-334 is `REVISION_READ_METHODS.has(method) ? true : attr.verb === 'rw' && !READ_GATED_METHODS.has(method)` — with `READ_GATED_METHODS = new Set(['AttachDocument'])` (line 108), an attach is now authorized as a read, which `hasAccess` grants any valid viewer link (line 370: `return needWrite ? link.role === 'editor' : true`).

Attack: an anonymous holder of a viewer-role share link POSTs the token to `POST /auth/yorkie-token/share` (auth.controller.ts:82) to mint a `yorkie-share` token, reads the project public key out of any visitor's bundle, then builds a bare `yorkie.Client`, creates a local `Document`, applies arbitrary local changes, and calls `attach`. Yorkie pushes that change pack as part of the AttachDocument RPC; the webhook is consulted with verb `rw` but answers ALLOW because attach is read-gated, so the pack is applied. Detaching and re-attaching repeats it without bound, so the "one pack per attach" bound is not a practical limit — a viewer has effective write access to the document on a fully enforcing deployment.

The change explicitly acknowledges this (`docs/design/yorkie-auth-webhook.md` § Risks, the READ_GATED_METHODS comment, packages/backend/README.md:222), and the public-template-gallery gate `assertYorkieAuthEnforced` now rests on a bound that is narrower than the role it advertises. I could not confirm the residual is closed anywhere else: `PushPull` is the only remaining write gate and it is reached only *after* the attach has already been applied. Flagging because a role check that was previously enforced is now not, and the surface it protects (every viewer-shared document, and every public template document whose `previewToken` is handed to every visitor) is the one the rest of the change argues is protected.

samples.summary: An unscoped `yorkie-service` token is a blanket read/write credential for every document in the deployment, and it is transmitted over the wire to a Yorkie server on every RPC
samples.evidence:
`decideService` returns `ALLOW` unconditionally when the token carries no `key` (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:289-291) — no method check, no attribute check. `signYorkieServiceToken` omits `key` whenever the caller does not pass one (yorkie-service-token.ts:66-69), which is exactly what `yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv()` does for `scripts/migrate-yorkie-cf-ranges.ts:221`, `scripts/migrate-yorkie-worksheet-shape.ts:347`, and both clients in `scripts/copy-yorkie-documents.ts:258,262`.

That token is not process-local: the SDK sends it to whichever Yorkie server `--source-rpc-addr`/`--target-rpc-addr`/`YORKIE_RPC_ADDR` names (default `http://localhost:8080`, i.e. plaintext), on every RPC, and `copy-yorkie-documents.ts` deliberately points one at a *different* deployment's Yorkie server. Anyone who observes it (MITM on a plaintext or misconfigured rpcAddr, a compromised or third-party-operated Yorkie server, a proxy/access log that records Authorization-style headers) holds, for its 10-minute lifetime, a credential the webhook answers ALLOW to for every method on every document key of the minting deployment — and the other half needed to use it, the project public key, ships in every visitor's bundle. The scoped variant used by `YorkieService.withDocument` bounds this to one document; the unscoped ops variant reintroduces exactly the blast radius the `key` claim was added to remove. No expiry shortening, no method restriction (`RestoreRevision`, `GetRevision` included) and no rpcAddr scheme check bounds it.

samples.summary: `key` is an optional trailing parameter, so the unsafe (unscoped, all-documents) token is what a caller gets by omission
samples.evidence: `yorkieServiceTokenInjector(secret, expiresIn = '10m', key?)` and `signYorkieServiceToken(secret, expiresIn, key?)` both treat an absent `key` as "authorize every document" (`decideService` short-circuits to ALLOW at yorkie-auth.controller.ts:289). The dangerous mode is therefore the default and the safe mode is opt-in — the inverse of the fail-closed direction the rest of this change argues for (`isYorkieAuthEnforced` is written specifically so a typo lands on the denying side). A future request-path client that forgets the third argument silently mints a deployment-wide credential and nothing — no type, no lint rule, no test — catches it; `yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv` does not even accept a `key`, so any new caller reaching for the convenience helper gets the unscoped one. A required explicit sentinel (e.g. `key: string | typeof UNSCOPED_OPS_TOKEN`) would make the blast radius visible at each call site.

samples.summary: Security documentation left asserting the now-inverted default: several docs and code comments still say the auth webhook ships in shadow mode and that the client-side read-only flag is the write boundary
samples.evidence: This change makes enforcement the default (`isYorkieAuthEnforced`) and corrects `docs/design/notes/notes.md`, `docs/design/yorkie-auth-webhook.md`, both READMEs and `packages/notes/src/store/read-only.ts` — but leaves the same claim standing elsewhere: `docs/design/sharing.md:208-219` ("This is **off by default**… in the default one the client-side `readOnly` flag is the write boundary rather than a convenience in front of one"), `docs/design/template-gallery.md:668` ("with `YORKIE_AUTH_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE` unset the auth webhook only *shadows*"), `packages/docs/src/store/read-only.ts:39-42` ("ships in shadow mode by default… this flag is the write boundary"), `packages/docs/src/view/editor.ts:4413`, and `packages/frontend/README.md:37`. `docs/design/sharing.md` is the canonical sharing threat model, and the notes sibling file explicitly records that believing this was "wrong, and worth recording as wrong". Leaving two authoritative documents disagreeing about which layer is the access-control boundary is how a later change ends up relying on the client-side gate — the exact mistake this branch documents. (Nested design docs are not link-checked by CI, and no lane checks prose consistency.)

samples.summary: The newly wired share-link image upload puts the access-granting share token in the URL query string, contradicting the project's own stated rule for that token
samples.evidence: `SharedNotesLayout` now hands `shareTokenImageUploader(token)` to `NotesView` (shared-notes-layout.tsx), which calls `postShareTokenImage` → `POST ${BACKEND_BASE}/api/v1/shared/images?token=${encodeURIComponent(token)}` (images.ts:57). The share token is a bearer credential granting anonymous edit access to the document, and the backend's own `POST /auth/yorkie-token/share` was deliberately made a POST-with-body for precisely this reason — auth.controller.ts:79-81: "Uses POST with the share token in the body so the (access-granting) token stays out of request URLs and access logs." A query-string token lands in reverse-proxy/CDN access logs, browser history, and `Referer` headers on any subresource the response triggers. The route pre-dates this change (added for the docs share surface), but this diff extends its use to note share links; the fix is to move the token to a header or body field, matching the auth controller.

samples.summary: Shadow-mode log line interpolates the client-influenced document key without sanitization (log-forging surface)
samples.evidence: The new `target` string is built from `attr?.key` and `attr?.verb` taken straight off the webhook body (lines 200-202) and interpolated into a single-line warn at line 204. The body is HMAC-verified as coming from Yorkie, and Yorkie constrains document keys, so I could not construct a concrete injection — but a key containing CR/LF or `status=`/`reason=` text would forge additional log records in a line-oriented log pipeline, and shadow-mode denials are precisely the records an operator uses to decide whether a deployment is safe to enforce. Escaping the key (e.g. `JSON.stringify`) removes the question. Correctly, the token itself is not logged.

verdict.reason: The described code exists verbatim: READ_GATED_METHODS = new Set(['AttachDocument']) (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:108) combined with needWrite = REVISION_READ_METHODS.has(method) ? true : attr.verb === 'rw' && !READ_GATED_METHODS.has(method) (lines 332-334) makes an AttachDocument authorized as a read, and hasAccess grants any valid viewer link on a read (line 370: `return needWrite ? link.role === 'editor' : true`). The repository itself documents this residual as open (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:99-106, docs/design/yorkie-auth-webhook.md:310-319, yorkie-auth-enforcement.ts:14-21), which corroborates rather than refutes the finding. Documented acceptance and the difficulty of fixing it without an upstream truthful verb do not close the viewer-to-writer authorization bypass, which is squarely in the access-control lane and critical by impact.

verdict.reason: Every claimed element is present and unguarded. yorkie-auth.controller.ts:289-291 returns ALLOW unconditionally for any yorkie-service token lacking `key`, positioned before the CLIENT_METHODS check, the fail-closed empty-attributes check (299-305), and the per-key comparison (306-314) — so no method or attribute is examined; RestoreRevision/GetRevision/PushPull on any document key are allowed. decide() routes all yorkie-service tokens there (241-243). signYorkieServiceToken omits `key` when none is passed (yorkie-service-token.ts:66-69), and yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv (104-116) never passes one, which is what migrate-yorkie-cf-ranges.ts:221 and migrate-yorkie-worksheet-shape.ts:347 use; copy-yorkie-documents.ts:53 likewise calls yorkieServiceTokenInjector(secret) with no key for both source (256) and target (261) clients pointed at two different deployments. rpcAddr defaults to plaintext http://localhost:8080 (cf-ranges:213, worksheet-shape:339) with no scheme check. The scoped path (yorkie.service.ts:78-88) does pass docKey and is bounded by controller:307, confirming the keyless variant bypasses exactly that bound. No guard removes it: AuthService.verifyYorkieToken (auth.service.ts:95-107) explicitly accepts YORKIE_SERVICE_TOKEN_TYPE, and `key` is optional in the payload type (yorkie-service-token.ts:54). In-lane (authorization scope + sensitive credential exposure) and major under this rubric; no not-present, already-guarded, or out-of-scope ground applies.

finding.summary: READ_GATED_METHODS lets a viewer-role share token write: the AttachDocument change pack is applied under a read-only decision
finding.evidence:
Pre-change, `checkAttribute` computed `needWrite = attr.verb === 'rw' || REVISION_READ_METHODS.has(method)`, so an `AttachDocument` (which Yorkie always sends with verb `rw`, per packages/backend/test/revision-history.e2e-spec.ts:373) required write authority. The new line 286 (`attr.verb === 'rw' && !READ_GATED_METHODS.has(method)`) drops that: attach is now authorized with `needWrite=false`, and `hasAccess` returns true for ANY viewer share link bound to that document (line 322: `return needWrite ? link.role === 'editor' : true`).

Full vector, all with public inputs: (1) an anonymous visitor loads a public template card and receives `previewToken` (template.service.ts:1314), which is a share link created with role `'viewer'` (template.service.ts:374); (2) POSTs it to the unauthenticated `POST /auth/yorkie-token/share` (auth.controller.ts:82) and gets a signed `{typ:'yorkie-share'}` token; (3) builds a bare `yorkie.Client` with the project public key that ships in every visitor's bundle, calls `doc.update(...)` on a local Document BEFORE `client.attach(doc)` so the mutation rides the attach ChangePack; (4) the webhook sees method `AttachDocument`, skips the write check, returns ALLOW, and the Yorkie server applies the pack. Detach + re-attach repeats it without limit.

So, even with `YORKIE_AUTH_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE` enforcing and every method registered, a read-only share link (and the gallery's preview token) is write-capable. That is precisely the consequence `assertYorkieAuthEnforced` (template-review.ts:104) gates the public tier on preventing — and the gate now attests something it no longer buys, since one attach per card is as cheap as the one request per card the gate's own comment describes. The change documents this as a "residual", but the weakening is introduced here in the same change that makes enforcement the default and re-opens the public tier on the strength of it; the accompanying claim that only a "non-browser client" can do it is not a security bo

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described. yorkie-auth.controller.ts:332-334 computes `needWrite = REVISION_READ_METHODS.has(method) ? true : attr.verb === 'rw' && !READ_GATED_METHODS.has(method)`, and READ_GATED_METHODS (line 108) contains 'AttachDocument', so an attach that Yorkie always sends with verb 'rw' is authorized with needWrite=false. hasAccess then short-circuits at line 370 (`return needWrite ? link.role === 'editor' : true`), so ANY viewer-role share link bound to that document passes the attach check. The identity is obtainable anonymously: POST /auth/yorkie-token/share (auth.controller.ts:82-89) carries no JwtAuthGuard — unlike GET /auth/yorkie-token at :68-72 — and mints a signed yorkie-share token from any share token; template.service.ts:374 creates the gallery preview link with role 'viewer' and :160-164 describes previewToken as that viewer token handed to listing viewers. Because Yorkie's AttachDocument RPC carries a ChangePack that the server applies, a non-browser client that mutates a local Document before attaching writes under a read-only decision, repeatable via detach/re-attach. No guard elsewhere closes this: PushPull is the only truthful write gate and it runs after the attach, and the frontend read-only mounts are acknowledged in-file (lines 124-130) as bounding only this app, not access control. The repository's own comments (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:99-106) and docs/design/yorkie-auth-webhook.md:310-319 concede the identical residual, which corroborates rather than refutes. Documenting a hole and having no easy alternative fix are not refutation grounds; this is an authorization weakness (read-only role gaining write capability) squarely in the security lane.

finding.summary: The `yorkie-service` token is an unscoped all-document read/write credential, and the rationale that it "never leaves the process" is false — it is transmitted to every Yorkie server the backend and the ops scripts talk to
finding.evidence:
`decide()` returns ALLOW for `identity.typ === 'yorkie-service'` before any document key, verb, attribute-presence or revision-method check runs, so one token authorizes read, write, `RestoreRevision`, and every other gated RPC on every document key in the deployment for its full 10-minute lifetime.

The security argument for that blast radius is stated in packages/backend/src/yorkie/yorkie-service-token.ts:24 — "it never leaves the process, so nothing but a secret compromise can produce one". That premise is wrong by construction: the token is exactly what `authTokenInjector` hands the Yorkie SDK, so it is sent over the wire to `YORKIE_RPC_ADDR` on every RPC (yorkie.service.ts:73), and copy-yorkie-documents.ts:258-262 deliberately sends one to a *different deployment's* Yorkie server. `YORKIE_RPC_ADDR` defaults to plain `http://` (yorkie.service.ts:31) and nothing forbids an http address across a network, so the credential can also travel in cleartext. Anywhere the Yorkie server or a proxy in front of it records request headers, that log now contains an all-documents read/write credential rather than a single user's.

The webhook body carries the document key it is deciding, so the token could have been minted bound to that key (`{typ:'yorkie-service', docKey}`) and compared in `checkAttribute`, bounding a leak to the document the server-side attach actually needed. As written there is no scoping of any kind. Confidence is medium because replaying the token at the webhook additionally requires a valid `YORKIE_SECRET_KEY` HMAC (yorkie-signature.guard.ts), so the practical holder is the Yorkie deployment and its logs rather than an arbitrary network attacker.

verdict.reason: The finding's central factual claims are not present in this repository. (a) `decide()` does not blanket-ALLOW service tokens: yorkie-auth.controller.ts:241-243 routes them to `decideService`, which at :306-314 returns 403 'service token is scoped to another document' for any attribute key != the token's key, and at :299-305 fails closed on a document-scoped method with no attributes. (b) The token IS scoped: `YorkieServiceTokenPayload.key` (yorkie-service-token.ts:33-55) is embedded by `signYorkieServiceToken` (:66-69), and every request-path client passes the per-document `docKey` (yorkie.service.ts:76-88). (c) The quoted rationale 'it never leaves the process, so nothing but a secret compromise can produce one' does not appear at yorkie-service-token.ts:24; that comment says the exact opposite (lines 24-28: 'it does **not** stay inside this process: it is handed to the Yorkie SDK... That is the reason for key'), i.e. wire transmission is the stated motivation for scoping. (d) copy-yorkie-documents.ts:40-54 mints each side's token from that side's own secret (SOURCE_JWT_SECRET/TARGET_JWT_SECRET) with no fallback, explicitly to avoid handing one deployment's credential to another (:69-74) — it does not send one deployment's token to a different deployment's server. The only remaining unscoped case is the ops-script operator credential (decideService:289-291), which requires possession of the deployment's JWT_SECRET (a compromise that already yields a session for any user) and is documented and unit-tested (yorkie-auth.controller.spec.ts:119-196). The claim 'As written there is no scoping of any kind' is false.
